lead: One week after Pentecost the Church turns from what God has done to who God is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The four readings of the feast do not give a definition; they show God acting. At Mamre, the Lord comes to Abraham as three visitors and is welcomed at a meal. In Isaiah, the God who is “the first and the last” speaks, and a mysterious voice says, “the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.” Paul shows the three at work in our lives: peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, and God’s love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. In John, Jesus says that the Spirit takes what is his, and that all the Father has is his. The words to watch are sent, poured and mine. The calendar also gives readings for the Second Sunday of the Apostles (Joel 2, Acts 4, 1 Corinthians 6, Luke 7); these notes follow the readings of the feast.

r.h: Three men by the oaks of Mamre
set: Abraham has settled by the oaks of Mamre near Hebron (13:18). God has promised him a son, but he and Sarah are old and still childless. In the heat of the day, when travel stopped, three men appear. The story continues after today’s reading with the promise that Sarah will have a son within a year (18:10), and in the next chapter two of the visitors, now called angels, go on to Sodom (19:1).

The narrator tells us at the start that it is “the Lord” who appears. Abraham sees three men. The text moves between singular and plural, and this has made the scene one of the most pondered pages of the Old Testament.
str: v. 1: the Lord appears at Mamre in the heat of the day.
v. 2: three men; Abraham runs to meet them and bows down.
vv. 3–5: he begs them to stay: water, rest, a little bread.
vv. 6–8: the great meal prepared in haste, and Abraham standing by them as they eat.
kw: In verse 3 Abraham speaks to one (“my lord… your servant”); in verses 4–5 he speaks to all three. The Jewish scribes who added vowels to the Hebrew text pointed the word as the divine title, Lord, showing that they understood Abraham to be speaking to God.
Abraham runs (vv. 2, 7) and hastens (vv. 6, 7) in the heat of the day, an old man serving strangers. Hospitality here is not a duty done slowly but love in a hurry.

Sarah kneads three measures of choice flour, far more than three guests could eat. Jesus’ parable of the yeast, read on Wednesday, uses the same measure (Matthew 13:33). God is welcomed with abundance.
vv: The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
God comes at an ordinary hour, to an ordinary tent. The Letter to the Hebrews remembers this scene: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).
He looked up and saw three men standing near him.
One Lord, three men. The Old Testament does not reveal the Trinity, but the Church has always seen in this meeting a shadow of what would be revealed in Christ.
Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
Abraham offers “a little” and gives a feast. The washing of feet will return, in a greater way, when the Lord himself washes the feet of his disciples (John 13:5).
and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
The host does not sit; he waits on his guests. The man to whom God made promises now serves God at table.
ch: Many Fathers saw in the three visitors a figure of the Trinity, and the Latin liturgy long sang a line often traced to St Ambrose: “He saw three, and worshipped one” (in substance). Others, such as St Justin Martyr, saw the Word of God with two angels. Both readings come from the same faith: the God who visits Abraham is the God who will make himself known as Father, Son and Spirit. The famous icon of St Andrei Rublev (early fifteenth century) shows the three at table with a cup in the centre. The Catechism sees in the hospitality at Mamre a prelude to the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571).

r.h: I am the first, and I am the last
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. God has raised up Cyrus, king of Persia, to release them. Chapter 48 closes the first half of these prophecies with a strong call to listen, and just after this reading comes the cry, “Go out from Babylon” (48:20).

In these verses God speaks as Creator and Lord of history. Then, in verse 16, a new voice is heard: someone sent by the Lord God, together with his spirit. Many scholars think it is the prophet himself, or the Servant of whom the next chapter speaks.
str: v. 12: “Listen to me”: I am He, the first and the last.
v. 13: the Creator of earth and heavens.
vv. 14–15: the one whom the Lord loves (Cyrus) will do his will against Babylon.
v. 16: “Draw near”; a voice: the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.
v. 17: the Redeemer who teaches and leads in the way.
kw: A short solemn formula in these chapters (41:4; 43:10). In the Greek Old Testament it is egō eimi, “I am”, which Jesus uses of himself in John’s Gospel (John 8:58).
God is before all things and remains after all. In the Book of Revelation the Risen Christ takes the same title: “I am the first and the last” (Revelation 1:17; 22:13).

In verse 16 the Hebrew can be read “the Lord God has sent me and his spirit”, with the spirit sent along with the speaker, or “has sent me, and his spirit has”. The phrase joins the Lord God, the one he sends, and his spirit.
vv: Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last.
God’s self-naming begins with a relationship: “whom I called”. The God of all ages is the God of a people.
My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens;
The Creator of all is not far away. The same hand that spread the heavens will lead the exiles home.
And now the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.

Many Fathers read this verse in the light of the New Testament: the Father sends the Son, and with him the Spirit. The prophet did not know the doctrine of the Trinity, but his words are open to the fullness God would reveal.
I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.
God teaches and leads. Jesus will promise a Spirit who “will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13), today’s Gospel.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God’s inmost being as Holy Trinity is a mystery that cannot be reached by reason alone, nor even by the faith of Israel before the Incarnation of the Son and the sending of the Spirit (CCC 237). Yet Israel’s faith in the one God, “I am He; I am the first, and I am the last,” remains the foundation. The Church confesses not three gods but one God in three Persons (CCC 253).

r.h: God’s love poured into our hearts
set: In chapters 1–4 Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles, need God’s saving justice, and that it is given through faith in Jesus Christ, as it was given to Abraham (chapter 4). Chapter 5 begins a new section: what life is like for those who have been justified. Paul writes to a Church he had not yet visited, in about AD 57.
str: vv. 1–2a: justified by faith, we have peace and access to grace through Christ.
v. 2b: we boast in hope of sharing God’s glory.
vv. 3–4: we boast even in sufferings: endurance, character, hope.

v. 5: hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Spirit. ¶ In five verses God, the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit are named, each at work in the believer.
kw: The word for being brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ we are led into the grace in which we now stand.
Literally the quality of something that has been tested and proved, like metal through fire. Endurance produces a tried and true character.
The verb is used of the Spirit “poured out” at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 33). The tense means poured once and remaining: the love of God is not a passing feeling but a gift that stays.
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

Textual note: the manuscripts differ by one letter. Many ancient ones read “let us have peace”; others read “we have peace”, which the NRSV follows. Our Malayalam translation reads it as an invitation. Both are true: peace is a gift, and we are to live in it.
through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand;
Grace is not a moment but a place where we stand. The access is “through” Christ: he is the door.
knowing that suffering produces endurance,
Paul does not boast of suffering for itself. He boasts because God can make it bear fruit.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
“God’s love” here means first God’s love for us, given and felt within. Christian hope rests on that gift, not on our own strength.
ch: The Catechism quotes Romans 5:5 when it teaches that God is love and that love is his first gift, containing all others, poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit (CCC 733). It also teaches that justification is the most excellent work of God’s love, given by grace through faith and Baptism, and that it truly makes us just from within (CCC 1987–1992, 1994). St Augustine returned to this verse again and again when he taught that grace is not only a law shown to us but love given to us (in substance, On the Spirit and the Letter).

r.h: The Spirit of truth will guide you
set: These verses come from Jesus’ farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–17). In it he speaks five times of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete (14:16–17, 26; 15:26; 16:7–11, 12–15). This is the last of these sayings. The disciples are grieving because Jesus is going away (16:6); he tells them that the Spirit will lead them further into what he has given.
str: v. 12: many things you cannot bear now.
v. 13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth; he speaks what he hears.
v. 14: he will glorify me, taking what is mine.
v. 15: all that the Father has is mine. ¶ The movement is from the Father to the Son to the Spirit to the disciples.
kw: To lead on the road, as a guide leads travellers (compare Psalm 25:5). The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel; he leads the Church deeper into the truth that is Jesus himself (14:6).
The verb is used three times in these verses. The Spirit announces, makes known, what he receives. He does not speak “on his own”.
In John truth is not only correct ideas; it is the reality of God made known in Jesus, who is “full of grace and truth” (1:14).
vv: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
Jesus respects the slowness of his disciples. Understanding will grow after Easter and Pentecost.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;

The Second Vatican Council teaches that through the Holy Spirit the Tradition that comes from the apostles develops in the Church, as there is a growth in understanding of the realities and words handed down (Dei Verbum 8).
He will glorify me, because he will take what is mine and declare it to you.
The Spirit always points to Jesus. A spirituality that leads away from Christ is not from this Spirit.
All that the Father has is mine.
One of the clearest words in the Gospels on the unity of the Father and the Son. What the Spirit gives us comes from the Father, through the Son.
ch: The Fathers used this verse against those who denied that the Son is equal to the Father: if all that the Father has belongs to the Son, the Son is God with the Father. The Catechism teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son; it explains that the Eastern tradition expresses this by saying he comes from the Father through the Son, and that, rightly understood, the two ways of speaking are complementary (CCC 246–248). St Ephrem compared the Trinity to the sun, its light and its warmth: distinct, yet one (in substance).

qa: Is the word “Trinity” in the Bible?

The word is not, but what it names is. The New Testament speaks of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as one God, as in the command to baptize “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) and in Paul’s blessing (2 Corinthians 13:13). The Church, guided by the Spirit of truth, found the words to confess this faith at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) (CCC 249–252).
Did Abraham see the Trinity at Mamre?

The text says that the Lord appeared and that Abraham saw three men. It does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity; that was revealed only in Christ (CCC 237). Some Fathers read the three as a sign of the Trinity, others as the Word of God with two angels. The Church allows both readings, and the icon of Rublev has made the first one beloved in East and West.
If God is three, how can he be one?

The Church does not say that God is one and three in the same respect. God is one in nature, one God, and three in Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who are really distinct in their relations to one another (CCC 253–255). It is a mystery, not a contradiction: reason cannot discover it, but it can see that it is not absurd.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar calendar the feast of the Most Holy Trinity falls on the Second Sunday of the Apostles, one week after Pentecost, and the calendar gives the Sunday’s own readings as a second set. Our Holy Qurbana is soaked in the praise of the Trinity. In the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari, which we pray through this season, the great prayer opens by praising the adorable and glorious Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who created the world by his grace.

The Season of the Apostles began with the Spirit poured out on the Church. Today we see where that gift comes from: from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Each time we make the sign of the Cross, or sing “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”, we name the God into whose life we were baptized.
study: Abraham ran to welcome strangers. Whom can I welcome this week as if I were welcoming God?
Isaiah’s God says, “I teach you for your own good.” Where do I need God to teach and lead me now?
Paul says suffering can produce hope. Name one present trouble and ask: what might the Spirit be forming in me through it?
How can my family pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit, more consciously at home?
